components.html:
If you are an experienced knitter or a "newbie" to machine knitting, this course is designed to introduce you to your machine, help you understand how it works and give you practice using it.

Don't practice till you get it right, practice till you can't get it wrong

Practice is the key word here. Just watching videos won't get it done. Schedule a bit of knitting time as often as you can to get more comfortable with your machine.

Think of it as a tool. When you learned to use a pencil it wasn't easy at first. Easy as it looks, driving a car takes more than just pressing on the gas and the brake.

Learning to machine knit is a combination of understanding your machine and mastering the techniques needed to create beautiful knitted items.

We want you to have success!

You are here because you want to learn more about your machine.
Make the most of the material presented. It is organized to be followed step-by-step. Work all the exercises and you will have a good foundation for taking the next steps on your machine knitting journey

We've created a checklist to help keep you on track. Download Checklist

lessons.title: Yarn and A Bit More Tech

components.html:
Another of the many features of the LK-150 is it's ability to knit a wide range of yarn weights.

When you knit, the weight and drape of the resulting fabric is determined by the Stitch Dial or Tension Dial.

These control the flow of the yarn through the carriage and the size of the resulting stitch. If you are a hand knitter, think of it this way, a larger needle will produce a large stitch, and therefore a more open knitted fabric. Also the weight of the yarn impacts the size of the stitch and the finished appearance of the knitted fabric.

With the LK-150 you can use a fine yarn- think of a sock weight yarn. or a #1. Because of the size of the hooks, the distance between the hooks and the setting of the tension dial, you can create very different fabrics even in plain stockinette knitting.

At the opposite end of the spectrum you can use a medium #4 weight yarn and create a hand knit look.

For heavier yarns, you even have the option of knitting over every other needle.

Something to consider ... the size of the hook of the needle determines the thickest yarn you can use. If you try to use a very bulky (or maybe a hand spun yarn) and it doesn't fit in the hooks of the needles, you'll be splitting the yarn and the stitches won't form properly.


  • Think of the Carriage Stitch/Tension Dial as the hand knitting needle size.

  • Think of the Mast Tension Dial as the tension a hand knitter would apply to the yarn with her fingers

blocks.title: Do you NEED yarn on cones?

components.html:
Do you need yarn on cones?

NO!

As long as the yarn will flow smoothly and evenly into the machine, you can use it!

slides.caption: Center-pull hand wound ball works great
Center-pull hand wound cake from a ball winder
If you can get them, cones work great ... plus fewer yarn ends to work in

components.html:
For your practice, choose:
  • Light Color
  • Smooth (no boucle or fuzzy yarn)
  • #4 weight (light worsted)
We will play with different yarns in another lesson. For now, when you are first starting out we recommend choosing a light color, medium weight, smooth yarn. Most of the #3 - or #4 yarns that you can get at craft stores will be good for practice when you get started.

Acrylic or acrylic blend are a great, affordable place to start. If you have access to wool, even better. Leave cotton and more expensive yarns aside when you are starting.

We want you to concentrate on learning your machine without worrying that you are wasting yarn. You will be working samples to hone your skills ... practice makes perfect, Practice is not wasting yarn!

Once you get a little experience with your machine, you can use yarns from your stash and get creative with your yarn choices. Taking baby steps is the best way to master your machine.

Understanding the position of the needles as you knit is important to mastering your machine. The position of the needles as you are knitting creates stitch patterns and short row shaping.

A: Out of work position
B: Working position
C: Middle Position
D: Hold position

It is the needle positions PLUS the settings of the levers on your carriage that control stitch patterning

Stitch patterning is not covered in this course . We will ONLY be working in stockinette. Unless otherwise instructed, the side levers will ALWAYS remain in this position



The position of the needles is controlled in 2 ways:

Manually positioning the needles by hand

This is a 1x1 needle pusher to select every other needle
Carriage Levers
Depending on the position of the needles, the carriage levers will automatically position the needles.

Tuck, Slip, Fairisle, Plaiting, Intarsia ... the possibilities are endless with your machine!

But ... we are going to focus on the basics.

Once you master the basics, stitch patterning will be a piece of cake!

Even if you have a little bit of experience with your machine, please don't skip this video.

Please take a few minutes to watch this video to the end.... you may pick up a tip of two ... plus the more you know about your machine, the more mastery you will have over it .... which translates to success!

When knitting across the full needlebed (100-150 stitches) it's helpful to use the Carriage Rests on each side of the needlebed.

This gives the carriage room to pass the edge of the knitting and form the stitches properly.

• Insert the Tension Rod Socket
  • Pull out the carriage rests
  • Clamp the machine to a sturdy table
  • Insert the tension rod
  • Snap the tension guide on the tension rod
  • Place the tensioner assembly on the top of the tension rod
  • Attach the row counter
  • Raise the carriage handle
  • Position the carriage on the needlebed
  • Confirm the carriage is seated correctly
  • Pass it back and forth with and without needles in work
  • Practice removing the carriage with the carriage release mechanism
Learning to do any sort of needlework feels clumsy at first.  I promise that threading up your machine will quickly become second nature to you.

We'll start with a very basic (and easy) cast on.  This method is great for swatching and playing, but it isn't exactly pretty.  Don't worry, at this point all we want to do is get stitches on the machine.  Practical and pretty cast on methods will be covered in a later section.

The goal:

Get started knitting and start exploring tension changes with the machine
  1. Practice threading your machine, securing the yarn tail in the yarn clip on the mast
  2. Confirm the carriage levers are set to plain knitting
  3. Set the carriage and mast tension to 5
    ------

  4. Put 50 needles (25 left and 25 right) in work (B-C or D position)
  5. Pass the carriage back and forth with no yarn
  6. Notice that the needles are all now in B (working) position
  7. Push all the needles to "A" (out of work position)
  8. Using your 1x1 needle pusher to pull every other needle into work (B-C or D position) (about 25 needles) 00:15
    ------

  9. Thread the carriage (#1 front slot) 00:35
  10. Position the carriage on the right
  11. Hold the yarn tail with one hand and pass the carriage from right to left (notice only the needles that were in work knit)
  12. Secure the yarn tail with a clip or clothespin 00:43
  13. Hang the cast on comb in the loops (catch every one) 01:08
  14. Put the out of work (A) needles into working position 01:38
  15. Knit Back
    ------
  16. Knit 10 rows at the current tension 01:49
  17. *Loosen the carriage tension by 1 number
  18. Knit 10 rows*
  19. Repeat from * to * until the carriage tension is at 9
  20. Knit a few more rows
    ------
  21. Remove the yarn from the carriage yarn feeder, pass the carriage across the knitting and drop the work from the machine
  22. Compare the different tensions. Which tension to do you prefer for your yarn?
Don't skip this video! The jump links in the numbered checklist refer to the video

sections.title: Tension
sections.bodyHtml:
We'll talk more about tension when we cover swatching, but for now, be aware of the tension setting on your machine in relation to the yarn you are using.

If stitches don't form correctly and seem really small, chances are the tension is too tight. Loosen up and try again
If stitches seem irregular, or the work drops off the machine, double check that they yarn is positioned correctly in the tension dial on the yarn mast.

sections.title: Master your Row Counter
sections.bodyHtml:
Machine knitters MUST count rows. We cannot measure the length of our knitting as it hangs on the machine.
Because the stitches are stretched between the needles and we hang weights as we are knitting, the fabric is distorted at first. (We'll talk more about this in the swatching section)
Your row counter makes easy work of keeping track of rows for you.

If you start your knitting at Row Counter (RC) 000 AND your carriage is on the right, it's easier to keep track of your rows. If the row on the counter is an EVEN number the carriage should be on the right.

sections.title: Knitting Fell off the machine @%^$!
sections.bodyHtml:
One of the most frustrating things for ALL machine knitters is the knitting falling off the machine. It WILL happen to you

If there is no yarn in the carriage (for a number of reasons) the knitting will fall off the machine:
  • You run out of yarn and don't notice
    Keep an eye on your yarn. You'll need AT LEAST 3x the length to complete a row. Stop; at the end of a row and start a new end of yarn. Leave the tails at the edge of the knitting to work in later.
  • The yarn breaks
  • The yarn isn't seated correctly in the carriage yarn feeder
  • The patterning levers are set incorrectly for the needle positions.
    For now, just keep checking that your carriage is set for plain knitting

sections.title: Loops or sloppy edges
sections.bodyHtml:
Taking the carriage too far past the edge of the knitting can cause loops.

Not taking it far enough can cause the knitting to fall off the machine.

If you rip out a row, or there's a lot of slack in the working yarn, pull down on the yarn behind the mast and re-engage the tension spring

sections.title: Knots in the yarn
sections.bodyHtml:
The tension guide can help when you have loose tangles coming from your ball or cone.

But knots in the yarn can get caught in the tension dial on the mast. They can also get caught in the carriage mechanism. The only way to prevent this is to re-wind your yarn, watching for knots as you are winding.

Unlike hand knitting, we can't feel a knot before it's knit and they are just a fact of life for machine knitters.

sections.title: Starting a new yarn
sections.bodyHtml:
We don't want to put knots in our knitting and then expect them to travel through the tension mast and the carriage.
If you are running out of yarn or you want to change colors:
  • At the edge of your knitting, remove the working yarn from the tension assembly and the carriage
  • Thread up the new end or color
  • Hold both ends in your hand or with a clip
  • Start knitting with the new strand
  • Work in the ends when you finish knitting

components.html:
Stockinette Stitch Curls. PERIOD


If you are a hand knitter, you may not have noticed this as much, but because machine knitters create perfectly formed stitches and exact tension throughout our knitting, the dreaded stockinette curl is much more noticeable.

It's NOT you

There are a few things that can "tame" the curl, but you aren't going to eliminate it.

  • Loosen up. The tighter the tension (and the knitting) the more it curls
  • Blocking helps
  • Knit a stitch pattern
  • Add hems and facings
  • Add trims - knitted or crocheted

You are making progress! ... we've spent a lot of time planning, practicing and thinking about knitting ... are you ready to do some "real knitting"?

DON'T SKIP THIS SECTION!

Your success with this course AND your success with your knitting machine depends on your understanding and mastering the art of knitting gauge swatches.

Without a swatch we are knitting in the dark.
  • How is the final sweater going to feel in the yarn and stitch pattern you've chosen?
  • Do you have enough yarn?
  • Do you have enough needles on your machine for the size you chose?

SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL

If you haven't used your chosen yarn before, how do you know the best tension to knit your project? 
Knitters tend to use the terms "tension swatch" and "gauge swatch" interchangeably, lets take a look at both.

GAUGE SWATCH

The gauge swatch is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.
It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.
TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.

TENSION SWATCH

When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric.

Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a tension swatch.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.

Let's practice knitting a tension swatch.

Play!

  1. Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.
  2. Knit 2-4 inches. Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)
  3. Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.
  4. Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.
  5. Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.
The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. At this point, you probably know exactly what you want to do with this yarn.  Knit your Gauge Swatch, dress it and and you are ready to design and knit your sweater.

Don't skip this!

Watch as we knit a "proper swatch".
Tips for casting on and binding off and placing markers and so much more!

components.title: How to Knit a Proper Swatch: The Secret to Machine Knitting Success

components.html:
Knitting a “Proper” Swatch

The goal of a swatch is to determine how many stitches and rows it takes to knit a 1” (or 4”/10cm) square.
To do this accurately, you will knit a larger piece, and mark of a set number of stitches and rows AS YOU KNIT.

After you dress (rest, wash, block) your swatch, you can easily measure and calculate your stitch and row gauge.
When you knit your swatch, you will cast on MORE stitches and knit MORE rows than shown. This will prevent you from measuring edge to edge and ONLY MEASURE the ISOLATED AREA.


  1. Garment yarn: Cast on 50 stitches with any method
  2. Knit for 1” or so - carriage on the right
  3. Contrasting waste yarn: Knit 2 rows
  4. Garment yarn: knit 20 rows
  5. Use a yarn marker or run a strand as you knit, isolate the stitches.
  6. Knit 20 rows
  7. Contrasting waste yarn: Knit 2 rows
  8. Garment yarn: knit 1” or so
  9. Bind off or drop the work from the machine
  10. Dress the swatch (wash, block and treat as you will the finished item)
Test Yourself

Accurate gauge swatching and accurate measuring is CRITICAL to your success as a machine knitter.

Test yourself with this exercise.

  1. Knit a "proper" swatch
  2. Let it rest, wash and block
  3. Carefully measure and calculate your gauge
  4. Calculate the stitches and rows for a 6" square
    1. Cast on {Stitches per inch times 6} stitches
    2. Knit {Rows per inch times 6} rows
  5. Knit a square according to your pattern
  6. Let it rest, wash and block
  7. Does your square fit in the template? Is it accurate? If not, double check your gauge measurements and try again.

The cast on method that you've been using (from your manual) is fast and easy, but it isn't appropriate for the finished edge of a "real" project.


An open cast on leaves "open" stitches that can be picked up later.
  • You might start a sleeve with an open cast on, then go back and pick up the stitches (by hand or machine) and hand knit ribbing.
  • You might pick up the open stitches and work a decorative bind off (by hand or machine)
  • Picking up the open stitches with crochet is another option
The most common method of creating an open cast on is with scrap yarn.


A closed cast on is a permanent finish that may be decorative or purely functional (like the "by the book" cast on)

There are many, many closed cast on methods. In the next section, we'll take a look at 2 of the most commonly used by machine knitters.

  • E-wrap cast on (stretchy and fast)
  • Chain (crochet) cast on (firm and decorative)

A preferred method of getting knitting on your machine is to "cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord". With this method, you add a few rows of knitting before starting your cast on with your garment yarn.


Benefits of Scrap 'n Ravel:
  • Use waste knitting to hang cast on comb and/or weights
  • Protect delicate/fine yarns
  • Immediately start patterning (tuck, lace, etc) with weights in place
  • Leave waste knitting in place to make blocking easier – especially for edges that roll
Overview of "scrap and ravel".


  • Work a fast cast on with waste yarn
  • Knit a few rows
  • Knit a row of ravel cord (so you can remove the scrap easily)
  • Start knitting with the garment yarn, safely leaving open stitches to be worked later
You'll practice this in the next section.
What is Ravel Cord?
Characteristics of Ravel cord
  • Similar weight to your garment yarn (or lighter)
  • Contrasting color
  • Smooth and slippery
  • Strong (you have to cut it and can’t break it with your hands)

Your machine may have come with ravel cord, but you can use anything that meets these criteria. Use your cord over and over, or toss it. It's your choice.

Having more than one cast on method in your toolbox is critical to mastering your knitting machine

As you work practice exercises (and knit swatches) in this course, use all 3 of these cast on methods.

Use the videos in the previous section and practice these cast on techniques.


e-Wrap Cast on (with waste yarn)

  1. Set carriage for plain knitting
  2. Put 20-30 needles into work
  3. With scrap yarn similar in weight to your garment yarn, ewrap cast on.
  4. Knit a few rows with scrap yarn. End on the LEFT
  5. Knit 1 row with ravel cord.
  6. Carriage on the right
  7. Starting on the left, with the garment yarn, e-wrap cast on over all the needles (over the ravel cord stitches)
  8. Thread your carriage
  9. Continue knitting
  10. Drop the knitting from the machine

Chain Cast On (with waste yarn)

  1. Cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord
  2. Starting on the left, follow the video
  3. Form a slip knot and place it on your latch tool
  4. Insert the tool between the first and second needle
  5. Catch the working yarn in the hook of the tool
  6. Pull the strand through the slip knot, forming a new loop.
  7. Keeping the loop in the hook of the tool, position the tool between the next 2 needles.
  8. Reach up and hook the working yarn again, pulling it through the loop on the hook. (This forms a chain)
  9. Continue to chain across all the needles
  10. Knit for a few inches
  11. Drop the work from the machine

Just like in hand knitting, there are many, many ways of binding off your knitting. From plain 'ol, functional bind offs to decorative edges machine knitters have lots of choices. Let's take a look at a couple of basics that are great with your machine.

sections.title: Drop the work from the machine
sections.bodyHtml:
When swatching or practicing, sometimes it's OK to just remove the yarn from the yarn feeder, pass the carriage across the needles in work and let the knitting drop from the machine.

Obviously these stitches can easily unravel, but if you are just playing, why take time to bind off?

No sound
Remove the yarn from the feeder and pass the carriage to drop the work from the machine


Simply dropping the work is often done when scrapping off your knitting.

By knitting a few rows of waste yarn, you safely maintain open stitches at the end of your knitting. These stitches can then be re-hung on the machine or picked up with hand knitting needles to finish the piece. (This is similar to using Scrap 'n Ravel cast on methods)

sections.title: Fast, Secure, Temporary Bind Off
sections.bodyHtml:
OK, if you are knitting a swatch and you are going to wash it, or you are going to handle your knitted piece a lot, Just leaving open stitches isn't practical you'll want to secure the stitches.

Running the tail of yarn through each stitch is a fast way to secure them.

No sound
Sometimes you have a very stretchy, open piece of knitting. Using a regular bind off method may distort the piece. Use this method to temporarily secure the stitches and avoid any distortion.

This is also a good technique for gathering the top of hats. Just run the tail through the stitches, pull tight and secure ... instant gathers!

sections.title: Back Stitch Bind off
sections.bodyHtml: Hand stitching creates a very stretchy bind off.

sections.title: Bind off by hand
sections.bodyHtml:
There is no rule that says you have to do EVERYTHING on the machine. If you are a hand knitter, you may want to take the stitches off the machine on a hand knitting needle and work the bind off method of your choice

No sound

sections.title: My Favorite Bind Off - Stitch thru Stitch
sections.bodyHtml: Stitch thru stitch bind off that is worked so YOU control the size of the bind off stitches and the tension of the bind off edge. Make it as firm or loose as you like. No guesswork.

components.html:
Take time to try different bind off methods while you are knitting swatches and practicing techniques. Don't get stuck using only one method.

Part of your journey to learn your machine is to learn different techniques and when to apply them.

Sadly patterns that are written specifically for machine knitting are few and far between. Most machine knitting patterns are cryptic (with tons of abbreviations) and dated.

With this course you are taking steps toward UNDERSTANDING your machine and learning to use it as a tool.

Part of that learning curve is understanding gauge. You may not want to design your own knitting patterns (you don't need to). BUT it is important that you understand how patterns are written and the importance of gauge to knit garments that fit. There is nothing worse than spending your time and energy knitting something and it doesn't come out the right size. Taking time to learn these concepts will GUARANTEE your success as a machine knitter.

If you've skipped the section swatching, promise me you will go back and review these lessons.
You WILL NOT HAVE SUCCESS unless you master swatching and gauge.

Ready to knit something useful?
The following lessons will help you put the concept of swatching and measuring accurate gauge to work.

I'm sure you are anxious to make something useful. We're going to take baby steps. Let's plan, design and knit some plain 'ol rectangles that can be used for scarves or shawls.

The skills, knowledge and confidence you gain will go a long way taking the next steps to make that fabulous sweater, coat or dress that you've been dreaming about.

blocks.title: Design A Blanket, Scarf or Shawl

components.html:
Scarves and small blankets* are just rectangles.

To knit one you need to know:
  1. What are the dimensions
  2. What is YOUR gauge
  3. How many stitches to cast on
  4. How many rows to knit
*When knitting blankets on the knitting machine, we are limited by the number of needles we have on the needlebed. To overcome this, machine knitters knit panels and join them.

To learn more about knitting larger blankets, check out the Knit it Now Course "DIY Blanket"
The course goes into depth covering designing your own blanket, knitting panels and finishing techniques.

Create your custom knitting blueprint

  1. Knit a swatch and establish YOUR Gauge
  2. Establish the length and width of your project
  3. Enter your info
  4. Click "Create Instructions" button for your pattern
